questions.explanation: `std::setw` applies only to the next formatted output and is then reset to zero, while `std::hex` and `std::setfill` stay in effect. The second `255` therefore prints in hex with no padding. The tempting `00ff 00ff` would need `setw(4)` repeated.

`operator>>` for an integer stops at the newline and leaves it in the stream. `std::getline` then reads up to that newline, producing an empty string, and consumes the newline. Discard the rest of the line with `in.ignore(...)` before calling `getline`.

The characters do not form a number, so the conversion fails: `failbit` is set and, since C++11, the value 0 is stored. The stream was not at the end of input when the failure was detected, so `eofbit` is clear. `badbit` is reserved for loss of integrity of the stream buffer, not for a parse error, and the old value 7 is not preserved.

After reading `3` the stream is not at EOF, because the newline is still unread, so `eof()` is false. The next `>>` skips the whitespace, reaches the end, and sets `eofbit` and `failbit` without storing anything, so `x` keeps the old value 3 and it is printed again. Testing `eof()` before reading is the bug; test the extraction itself with `while (in >> x)`.

To know that the number has ended, the extraction must try to read one more character, and it finds the end of input. That sets `eofbit`, but the extraction itself succeeded, so `failbit` is clear and `x` is 42. This is why `eof()` alone cannot tell you whether the last read worked.

`str()` replaces the buffer contents but does not touch the stream's state bits. The first read left `eofbit` set, so the second extraction's sentry fails, sets `failbit`, and leaves `x` at 42. Call `in.clear()` after `str(...)` to reuse the stream.

options: `1,2,` then `done`, because `eofbit` is not in the mask
questions.explanation: The idiomatic loop ends because the third extraction sets `failbit`. With `failbit` in the exceptions mask, setting it throws `std::ios_base::failure` instead of returning a stream that converts to false. The `done` line is never reached. The `eofbit` is set too, but it is the `failbit` that matches the mask.

The numeric extraction converts with the rules of `strtoull`, which accepts a leading minus sign for unsigned types and negates the result modulo the type's range. So `-1` becomes the maximum value and no failure is reported. The tempting `0 1` assumes the library rejects a negative number for an unsigned target; it does not.
